PyTorch 2.5.1 explicitly warns that batched computations and singleton computations can produce different floating-point results despite mathematical equivalence. Thus, small packed-GRU batch-versus-singleton differences alone do not establish a padding or checkpoint bug; disabling TF32 does not guarantee bitwise equality across batch shapes. This is an inference from the general numerical-accuracy guarantee, not a documented GRU-specific error bound. [Version-pinned numerical-accuracy documentation](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v2.5.1/docs/source/notes/numerical_accuracy.rst).

In 2.5.1, `torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32` defaults to `False`, while `torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32` defaults to `True`. These are separate controls; documentation explicitly lists GRU/LSTM among affected modules. Setting both to `False` provides a useful full-FP32 diagnostic comparison, but results measured under those settings do not establish deployment behavior unless the predictor applies the same settings. TF32 permission also does not prove a particular kernel actually used TF32. [Version-pinned CUDA documentation](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v2.5.1/docs/source/notes/cuda.rst).

Precision and determinism address different issues. Seed 42 alone does not eliminate CUDA nondeterminism; PyTorch documents deterministic-algorithm controls and CUDA workspace configuration separately. Practical implication: compare repeated identical calls first, then compare batches against singleton calls using the actual deployment precision, packing, device and inference mode. Report numerical tolerances and ranking changes separately; deterministic execution does not promise equality between differently shaped computations. [Version-pinned reproducibility documentation](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v2.5.1/docs/source/notes/randomness.rst).
